title: Diabetes, Weight Loss and Fatty Stools / Replace Enzymes, Support Alcohol Cessation, Protect Bones

blocks.text: Diabetes, Weight Loss and Fatty Stools / Replace Enzymes, Support Alcohol Cessation, Protect Bones

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-29 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) · 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min · Guidelines: NICE NG104 Pancreatitis (published 5 September 2018; last updated 16 December 2020); NICE CG115 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis, assessment and management of harmful drinking (high-risk drinking) and alcohol dependence (published 23 February 2011; last updated 21 October 2014) · Related AMaC: Consultation: chronic diarrhoea and weight loss; abnormal liver tests

Dear Doctor, a 54-year-old former publican. Diabetes for a year with poor control, weight loss and pale loose stools. Upper abdominal pain through to the back. Calcification seen on a scan. Please assess and advise.
Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Diabetes, weight loss and fatty stools with pancreatic calcification mean chronic pancreatitis with exocrine and endocrine failure; treat both and address alcohol.

The Examiner Trap. He sees only the diabetes. Candidates increase the diabetes tablets and miss the malabsorption. Pass: replace enzymes, review diabetes, advise on alcohol and plan monitoring. Fail: adjust the diabetes tablets alone.

rows: Pancreas or small bowel? Get the story.

BMI, muscle wasting, pallor, bruising, abdomen, mass, jaundice, ascites.

Enzyme replacement; dietitian; diabetes; vitamins; bone density; alcohol.

Chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency and pancreatogenic diabetes
Chronic pancreatitis against coeliac disease and pancreatic cancer, not assuming alcohol is the cause

Enzyme replacement; dietitian; diabetes review; asks about the pain and offers analgesia with a review of how well it works; assesses dependence and arranges supported alcohol cessation; no abrupt unsupervised withdrawal; bone density
Adds specialist pain team and pancreatic team input if the pain persists, monitoring of vitamin and mineral deficiencies, insulin assessment and a safety net for jaundice or weight loss

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are. A 54-year-old former publican. Weary, defensive about alcohol, thin. Lives alone.
Opening line. "My sugar's been all over the place. The tablets don't seem to help."
Volunteered. Diabetes for a year; weight loss; belly pain that goes through to your back.

Only if asked. Pale, greasy, floating stools that are hard to flush. Lost about 10 kg (scenario). Drinks about a bottle of spirits a day for many years; you have cut down a little. Smoker. No jaundice. No vomiting. No family cancer. No allergies. You take metformin for the diabetes and paracetamol when the pain is bad, which helps a little. The pain is there most days, about 5 out of 10, worse after meals, and sometimes wakes you at night. No recent travel. You do not drive today.
Hidden concern. You fear it is pancreatic cancer and that you will be blamed for drinking. Reveal only if asked what worries you most.
Your questions. "Is it cancer?" "Do I have to stop drinking?" "Will I need insulin?" "What are the tablets for?"
How you react. Good handling: you open up about alcohol and accept help. Poor handling: if lectured you say you will stop attending.

Findings (released as each step is done). Thin, BMI 18 (scenario). Muscle wasting. Mild epigastric tenderness, no mass. No jaundice, ascites or hepatomegaly. HbA1c high; faecal elastase low (scenario values). Calcification in the pancreas on a scan.

Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency and diabetes. Q2 Cause (R5): do not assume it is alcohol-related just because he drinks (NICE NG104 1.3.2). Q3 Treatment (R6): enzyme replacement per protocols agreed with the specialist pancreatic centre (1.3.4); dietitian assessment (1.3.5); pain: ask about severity and its effect on sleep, eating and mood, offer analgesia per BNF or local protocol with early review, and involve the local pain team and the specialist pancreatic centre if it persists (1.1.3); neuropathic pain follows the NICE neuropathic pain guideline (1.3.13); monitor malnutrition and deficiencies yearly (1.3.20). Q4 Diabetes (R6): HbA1c at least every 6 months (1.3.25); assess for insulin (1.3.15). Q5 Bones and alcohol (R7): bone density every 2 years (1.3.21); advise him to stop drinking (1.1.8) with assessment of dependence and assisted withdrawal if needed (NICE CG115).
Curveball 1. "He now has jaundice." (R6) Safe: urgent assessment for a bile duct stricture or cancer.
Curveball 2. "He is dependent on alcohol." (R7) Safe: supervised withdrawal is safer than stopping suddenly alone.
Curveball 3. "Are enzymes taken with food?" (R6) Safe: yes, with meals and snacks, titrated by the specialist team.
Curveball 4. "He refuses to cut down." (R7) Safe: explore, support, document; revisit.

Fail performance
CANDIDATE: You drink too much. [R1 Fail] (No stool or weight history. [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail])
(Reports a mass and jaundice that are not there. [R4 Fail])
CANDIDATE: It's coeliac disease. [R5 Fail] Take more diabetes tablets. [R6 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Stop drinking, starting today. [R6 Fail] [R7 Fail]

Examiner note: Blaming, no history, signs invented. Diabetes tablets alone leave malabsorption untreated, and telling a man who drinks a bottle of spirits a day to stop at once with no withdrawal plan is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): withdrawal can cause seizures.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello. May I ask questions and examine you? Any pain? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Tell me about the pain, stools, weight, alcohol and smoking. How is the diabetes treated? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Greasy stools, a bottle a day. I'm afraid it's cancer.
CANDIDATE: That's a real worry. What concerns you most? [R3 Pass]
(Checks nutrition and abdomen gently, then covers him; thin, epigastric tenderness, no mass. [R4 Pass])
CANDIDATE: This looks like chronic pancreatitis with diabetes. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: I'll start enzyme tablets with meals, refer to a dietitian, review your diabetes, arrange a bone mineral density assessment and assess dependence and arrange supported alcohol cessation; do not stop abruptly without a withdrawal plan. For the pain, I will find out how bad it is, offer pain relief and review how well it works. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Enzymes help digestion and weight; supported alcohol cessation can reduce further harm. What would you like me to explain further? [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and clear. Did not name alternatives or monitoring detail.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello. May I ask questions and examine you? Any pain? [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Tell me about the pain, stools, weight and alcohol. How is the diabetes treated? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Would you like pain relief first? I'll be gentle. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any earlier pancreatitis, jaundice or family history? How did the drinking begin? [R2 High]
PATIENT: I'm afraid it's cancer and you'll blame me.
CANDIDATE: Thank you for telling me. We'll check carefully, and I'm here to help, not blame. [R3 High]
(Checks nutrition and abdomen; thin, epigastric tenderness, no mass. [R4 High])
(Also checks pallor, bruising and ascites; no jaundice, mass or ascites. [R4 High])
CANDIDATE: Chronic pancreatitis; coeliac disease and pancreatic cancer are alternatives, and I won't assume alcohol alone. [R5 High]

CANDIDATE: I'll start enzyme tablets with meals, refer to a dietitian, review your diabetes, arrange a bone mineral density assessment and assess dependence and arrange supported alcohol cessation; do not stop abruptly without a withdrawal plan. [R6 High]

CANDIDATE: Enzymes per protocols agreed with the pancreatic centre, dietitian review, yearly checks for vitamin and mineral deficiencies, HbA1c every six months, insulin assessment, bone density every two years. If the pain persists I will ask the pain team and the pancreatic specialists for help. Return with jaundice or further weight loss. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: Options: enzymes now, or not and risk malnutrition. Because you drink heavily, stop with supervised support rather than suddenly alone. What would you like me to explain further? [R7 High]
Examiner note: Answered the fear of blame and cancer and covered monitoring.

R6: Raising the diabetes tablets alone leaves malabsorption and weight loss untreated. Telling a heavy daily drinker to stop at once with no withdrawal plan is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): withdrawal can cause seizures.
R2: No alcohol or stool history misses the cause and the steatorrhoea.
R4: Reporting a mass or jaundice not present shows signs were assumed.
R5: Coeliac disease ignores pancreatic calcification and pain through to the back.
R1: Lecturing about alcohol first makes him defensive.
"Tell me about your stools and your weight."
"I won't assume it's the alcohol alone."
"What worries you most?"

NICE NG104 (published 5 September 2018; last updated 16 December 2020): do not assume chronic pancreatitis is alcohol-related just because a person drinks (1.3.2); advise people with alcohol-related pancreatitis to stop drinking (1.1.8). NICE CG115 (2011; last updated October 2014, section 1.3.4): consider assisted withdrawal for people who typically drink over 15 units a day or score 20 or more on AUDIT.
Enzyme replacement by protocols agreed with the specialist pancreatic centre (1.3.4); dietitian assessment (1.3.5); monitor exocrine insufficiency and malnutrition at least every 12 months (1.3.20).
HbA1c at least every 6 months (1.3.25); assess for insulin every 6 months in type 3c diabetes (1.3.15); bone density every 2 years (1.3.21).

The scenario already strongly suggests alcohol dependence: assess last drink, withdrawal symptoms, prior seizures and available support; arrange safe medically assisted withdrawal rather than abrupt cessation alone. Ask about pain at every visit: assess severity and its effect, offer analgesia per BNF or local protocol with review, and seek the pain team and pancreatic centre if it persists. Give pancreatic enzymes with meals and snacks and review response with dietetics and the pancreatic team. Type 3c diabetes carries hypoglycaemia risk, especially with malnutrition or insulin; plan diabetes education and monitoring. Persistent or worsening weight loss, changed pain or jaundice requires reassessment for pancreatic cancer or complications despite existing calcification.
THINK: Chronic pancreatitis; exocrine and endocrine failure.
SAY: "Your pancreas isn't making enough digestive juice; tablets with meals can help."
DO: Enzymes; dietitian; pain plan; diabetes; bone density; alcohol support.
NUMBERS: BMI 18, 10 kg lost (scenario); HbA1c six-monthly, bone density two-yearly (NICE NG104).
TRAP: Diabetes tablets alone.
FINISH: Safety net: jaundice, weight loss.
